summary: Find the water cell with the greatest Manhattan distance to its nearest land cell, or -1 if there is no land or no water.
mainInsight: Start one BFS from all land cells together. The first time a water cell is reached gives its nearest land distance, and the last BFS level is the answer.
invariant: When level d is processed, the queue holds exactly the cells whose nearest land is at distance d, each enqueued once.

approaches.name: BFS from each water cell
approaches.summary: For every water cell, BFS until land is found.

approaches.name: Distance DP in two passes
approaches.summary: Sweep top-left to bottom-right and back, relaxing distances from neighbours.

approaches.name: Multi-source BFS
approaches.summary: Queue all land cells and expand level by level.
weaknesses: Needs the all-land and all-water guard

personalSolution.approach: Multi-source BFS reusing the grid to store distance + 1
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. calDis always returns 1 for neighbouring cells, so it can be removed, and a level counter avoids encoding distance + 1 in the input grid.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the all-land and all-water cases.
Marking visited when popped, causing duplicate queue entries.
Returning the number of levels instead of levels - 1 (off by one).
Running a separate BFS for each water cell.
edgeCases: Single land cell in a corner.

cards.answer: Multi-source BFS that starts from all land cells at once. Clue: Each water cell needs its distance to the nearest land cell on a grid, which is a shortest-steps question from many sources, so all land cells can start the search together.
keyPoints: Each water cell needs its distance to the nearest land cell on a grid, which is a shortest-steps question from many sources, so all land cells can start the search together.
cards.explanation: Nearest-source distances on a grid come from a single BFS whose initial queue holds every source.

rubric.technique: Multi-source BFS that starts from all land cells at once
aliases: bfs from every land cell simultaneously

alsoValid.name: Run a BFS from every water cell until it reaches land
alsoValid.note: correct, but repeats the search for each water cell and costs far more than one pass

alsoValid.note: correct, but quartic in the grid side

rubric.clue: Each water cell needs its distance to the nearest land cell on a grid, which is a shortest-steps question from many sources, so all land cells can start the search together.

promptVariants: Why is one BFS from all land cells enough to answer for every water cell?
How do you get the answer out of a multi-source BFS?
cards.answer: Put every land cell in the queue at distance 0. BFS reaches cells in non-decreasing distance, so the first time a water cell is reached is via its nearest land cell. The farthest water cell is therefore reached in the last BFS level, and that level number is the answer.
keyPoints: Answer is the number of the last level
cards.explanation: Reversing the direction (from land to water) turns many searches into one.

promptVariants: Why is a cell marked as seen when it is enqueued rather than when it is popped?
What goes wrong if cells are marked only when popped?
options: A cell would be queued by several neighbours and processed repeatedly
A cell would get the wrong distance because levels would be skipped
The first land cell would never be popped from the starting queue
A cell on the border would be missed by the bounds check entirely
cards.answer: A cell would be queued by several neighbours and processed repeatedly
cards.explanation: Several cells of one level can reach the same neighbour before it is popped. Marking on enqueue guarantees each cell enters the queue once, which keeps the work at O(n^2).

incorrectOptionExplanations.A cell would get the wrong distance beca: Distances stay correct; only duplicate queue entries and wasted work appear.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The first land cell would never be poppe: Land cells are popped normally; marking time concerns water cells.
incorrectOptionExplanations.A cell on the border would be missed by: The bounds check is independent of when cells are marked.

promptVariants: For which input is no answer defined?
cards.explanation: With no land cell the queue starts empty, and nothing has a nearest land. An all-land grid has no water cell either; both return -1.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[1, 0], [0, 0]]: One land cell and three water cells: the farthest water is at distance 2.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[0, 1], [1, 0]]: Every water cell touches land, so the answer is 1.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[0, 0], [0, 1]]: Land exists, so water cells have a nearest land; the answer is 2.

promptVariants: In your BFS, what does `self.calDis((r, c), (nr, nc))` return and what does the grid cell store afterwards?
cards.answer: Neighbouring cells are always at Manhattan distance 1, so calDis is just 1 and the helper is redundant. Land cells hold 1, so a water cell stores (distance + 1), which is why the final answer is best - 1. The grid is reused as the visited marker, which mutates the input.
keyPoints: Cells store distance + 1 because land is 1
Grid is mutated as visited marker
cards.explanation: Encoding distance in the grid is neat but hides the +1; a separate seen array or level counter is clearer.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code for an n x n grid?
Derive the running time from the BFS.
cards.explanation: Each of the n^2 cells enters the queue at most once and each is expanded with four constant-time neighbour checks.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^4): That is a separate search from each water cell, or all pairs of cells.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^3): That would come from a BFS or scan per row or per column.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^2 log n): A plain deque BFS has no logarithmic factor; there is no heap.

promptVariants: The queue and the seen matrix together hold O(n^___) cells in the worst case.
Extra space of the BFS on an n x n grid: O(n^___).
cards.explanation: The seen matrix has n^2 cells and the queue can hold a large fraction of them.
